Remarks by Jay McEntee:

This recording comes from a collection of Bob Campbell's recordings that were donated to the University of Florida by Campbell's widow, Heather Campbell, in February 2015. See details at: http://www.library.ufl.edu/spec/manuscript/guides/campbell.htm. The recording can also be accessed directly from the University of Florida at: http://ufdc.ufl.edu/AA00050139/. Please contact Daniel Reboussin (danrebo at uflib dot ufl dot edu) with any questions about the rest of this collection. Also note the preferred citation for this material: [Identification of item], Bob Campbell Papers, Special and Area Studies Collections, George A. Smathers Libraries, University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida.

Campbell made this recording in the first year (1968) he visited Dian Fossey's Karisoke Camp, which she established in 1967. The tape was labeled "Field recording of gorilla vocalizations, chest beating and other". The recording was included by UF librarian Daniel Reboussin in a display of Campbell's documentation of Karisoke, commemorating the 50th anniversary of its establishment.

The song bout captured in the recording has the form of double-collared sunbird territorial bout singing, with a series of short calls interspersed with silence leading to a ~2 - 5s long complex trill-like component. It seems there are at least 5 possibilities for the source of the song: Northern Double-collared Sunbird Cinnyris reichenowi, Olive-bellied Sunbird Cinnyris chloropygius, Regal sunbird Cinnyris regia, Ruwenzori Double-collared Sunbird Cinnyris stuhlmanni, and Rockefeller's Sunbird Cinnyris rockefelleri. Based on song recordings of the first three on xeno-canto, I do not believe any are a match. I have not been able to find recordings of territorial bout singing, as is heard in the recording, of either C. stuhlmanni or C. rockefelleri. As C. stuhlmanni appears to be common in the Virunga Mountains, whereas C. rockefelleri is not, I suggest C. stuhlmanni is far more likely. According to Cheke and Mann's book Sunbirds (2001), the local race of C. stuhlmanni is C. s. graueri.

Observation of a male and two females after searching for long minutes for the origin of unidentified calls. Perched above me and visibly very disturbed by my presence, the male was the least mobile and perched lowest (about 5m). He tried several times to intimidate me by bristling his hair and shaking a branch  with his 4 limbs while emitting 3 warning calls, sometimes accompanied by grunts. The females, perched higher up, were the most nervous and constantly moved from one branch to another while never taking their eyes off me. These are the ones uttering very high-pitched "clacking" calls. The scene lasted for several minutes after which I moved away (I had disturbed them enough as it was).

I live in the West Island of Montreal, and for the past few weeks, I’ve been hearing this animal near the corner of my house where my bedroom is. I live in a single-family home.

There are no holes in the soffits or in the roof vents. Right at that spot, however, there is a gutter downspout. All of my gutters are equipped with leaf guards along their entire length, so I’m wondering if the animal could be climbing up the downspout and hiding in the gutter, sheltered under the guard. I always hear the exact same sound; the volume varies, but it consistently seems to come from that same location.

I did previously have a single mouse in my house, but an exterminator inspected the entire property, including the attic, and found nothing unusual. I even mentioned this sound to him, and he checked the attic right above that specific spot but didn't notice anything.
I think I am hearing a jaguar in the jungle of Costa Rica near Lake Arenal. But I don't know. It might be a howler monkey.

I live in remote ranch country in Deep South Texas, about 60 miles north of the USA/Mexican border. I clearly heard the sound from inside. I went outside to investigate and my two dogs were standing still and quiet, staring intently in the direction of the sound, which was to the west. I brought them inside and returned outside, all the while listening to the sound. I turned on the audio recording application in my iPhone and recorded 30 seconds of the sound. I walked toward the location from where the sound came but it stopped and never repeated the rest of the evening. I do not believe it was a bird, but a medium-sized mammal, perhaps a fox, bobcat, or mountain lion, all of which are known to this area.

The recording is not altered in any way. The wind was blowing steadily because a rainstorm was approaching. The vegetation is Texas thorn-scrub brush with mostly mesquite trees but some Texas ebony and huisache trees as well. The area has been in severe drought so there was just a little bit of live grass in the understory.

It documents nicely how this squirrel started with the low chucks, switched to higher chuckes wich slowly were grouped in well-speced bursts of calls. All came from the same indiviudual, which I managed to photograph only badly. It can be separated from Pallas's Squirrel by the light pinkish eye-ring, the absence of rusty brown in the face, and the slightlt browner colour on the top of the dorsum. rmk:
Three buzzing noises that came from an echidna I startled when I walked past it on a trail. These buzzes are best seen on a spectrogram using a window length around 300, since the oscillation speed of the buzz is fast at around 13 milliseconds. The echidna was located under a tuft of ferns and climbing grass. I couldn't see it vocalizing, so there's a chance that this wasn't a sound the echidna made, however the sound was coming right from where its head was located. When I first noticed the echidna as it startled, it made one buzz noise like this. So I took out my recorder and captured these next 3 buzzes at 0:00, 0:03, and 0:06. Then it made two more buzzes before I left. It's unclear whether these sounds were vocalizations or an artifact of its breathing, like a wheeze or snort.

I totally wanted to be the first person to post an echidna recording on Xeno-canto, so here it is folks, wahooooo!

rmk:
House mouse (*Mus musculus*): A House mouse eats banana in a kitchen. 
This is my "retaliation" to a House mouse who chose to move in with us in winter 2023/24. Since then, it resides in the kitchen and eluded successfully the life-traps I have put up to repatriate it to nature. A very clever and discrete mouse indeed! I assume it is a female, as it doesn't smell like mouse in the kitchen, but I can't say for sure, though I have seen it on a few occasions. As it causes not much mayhem, we let it live with us. But, I wanted it to be documented, so I put up the recorder extremely close to a banana, as the mouse loves to eat banana (or other fruit as well). 

I wasn't sure if the recorder would capture the usually high frequencies of mouse calls, I was rather surprised that it did register frequencies up to 40 kHz! Don't expect too much of it, the sensitivity in these extreme frequency bands is low, and I would not expect it to register calls of bats or other animals, If you don't get real close to them. It worked out only because of the close distance (say three to five centimeters) to the mouse and some thoughtful editing (see below), and thus you can hear it munching, and there are some faint eeks and whistles towards the end of the clip. They can be heard much better in the modified version of the recording. However, I suggest using good headphones to hear them, and please listen closely. The sounds are there. I will have another go with another set-up including a better recorder with a much more sensitive microphone connected to it.

This is a version of XC999552 lowered by three octaves (87.5%). The speed, however, has not been changed, so the duration is the same as the in the original file. The calling and eeking should be heard easier in the lower register, now.

Perched on tall tree in deciduous forest. About an hour after sunset, already to dark to see who's talking to me. I guess it might be a Pine Marten _Martes martes_. High-pass filter 75 Hz 48 dB, Volume +10 dB.

The solution of the mystery came via Stefanie Huck <https://fb.com/retscheiderhof> / <https://www.retscheider-hof.de>. These calls are a combination of excitement and menacing calls of a scared Beech Marten _Martes foina_. 

It was an interesting experience to be in the nightly forest with an unknown grouchy creature right above me on a tree. I definitely was scared, too...

The expertise of Stuart Newson about this particular recording:

"I don’t think that these were produced by a Sorex species, as you note, the calls are too slow. I also considered Nyctalus noctula social calls (trills) briefly, but haven given this some thought, I don’t think that these were produced by Nyctalus noctula either.

I also considered the ‘mouse’ call of Cyanistes caeruleus – these calls are like slowed down shrew calls like these, but having a check, the calls here are too high in frequency for this species to be possible.

That brings me on to what I think is the most likely possibility, that these were produced by a Crocidura species. In the Netherlands, I have done a lot of work on the sound identification Crocidura russula, but it very rarely produces pronounced trills in its calls – I don’t think that I can completely exclude this possibility, but I would be surprised if they were produced by this species.

This leaves me with Crocidura leucodon. This is the only shrew species in the Netherlands I think, where I have only seen a small number of recordings and I don’t understand its vocalisations.

I think in summary I think that the calls here were most likely to have been produced by a Crocidura species – perhaps Crocidura russula, but it would be good to know if C. leucodon is present in your part of the country to see if this species is possible."

"I discussed and showed these recordings with a colleague of mine Simon Gillings today, which further confirmed my thinking that the calls here couldn't have been produced by a bird species."

Hello!
